extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and epistemological philosophy (general readers of philosophical treatises)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate claims that certain speculative or practical principles are 'innate' (imprinted on the mind). The page presents proposed marks for innateness, illustrative counterexamples, and tests one can apply (empirical, conceptual, and historical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal assent / knowledge requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a practical principle is innate it must be known and assented to by every one (infallibly) — innate principles cannot be such that any person could be ignorant of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that it is impossible that a whole nation publicly renounce a rule which every one of them certainly and infallibly knew to be a law. If a principle were truly innate, all would recognize it and publicly approve; the presence of widespread dissent or ignorance indicates non-innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally allowed breach disproves innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The generally allowed breach of a rule anywhere is proof that it is not innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Parents, preserve and cherish your children' — widespread practices (exposure, infanticide, eating children in some societies; ancient Greeks/Romans exposing infants) show the rule is commonly and permissively broken, so cannot be an innate imprinted law. Hume uses empirical instances from various cultures to illustrate this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate principles must be propositions (capable of truth), not commands
rubrics_metrics.description: A putative innate rule must be a proposition (capable of truth or falsehood); mere commands (imperatives) are not truths and thus cannot be innate knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume points out that moral injunctions like 'Parents preserve your children' are commands; to treat them as innate one must recast them as propositions ('It is the duty of parents to preserve their children'), which presupposes ideas of law, a lawgiver, reward and punishment — all of which would themselves have to be innate for the duty to be innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innateness entails innate auxiliary ideas (God, law, punishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a duty/proposition is innate as a truth about obligation, the mind must also carry innate ideas of law, a lawmaker, reward/punishment, and an afterlife; otherwise 'duty' cannot be apprehended as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that practical duties presuppose a conception of law and sanction; therefore claiming duties are innate implicitly requires that complex metaphysical and theological ideas be innate as well — a heavy burden for the innateness thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty test: innate principles must secure certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate principles are supposed to give certainty; if people can be ignorant or doubtful of them, then they fail to provide the promised certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume reasons that if something were truly innate and imprinted, people would have an indubitable knowledge (including certainty of punishment for violation). The observed ignorance and doubt about alleged innate rules undermines their role in securing certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to specify / catalogue innate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who assert innate principles should be able to state which principles they claim are innate; absence of any definitive catalogue is evidence against the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume notes that defenders of innateness are 'sparing to tell us WHICH THEY ARE.' If principles were truly innate, their number and identity should be obvious and easy to list — the failure to do so suggests the claim is dubious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herbert’s marks (Notitiae Communes) for innate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord Herbert's six marks purportedly identifying innate/common notions: 1. Prioritas. 2. Independentia. 3. Universalitas. 4. Certitudo. 5. Necessitas (faciunt ad hominis conservationem). 6. Modus conformationis (Assensus nulla interposita mora).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume reproduces Herbert’s list and then subjects it to scrutiny — treating these marks as an explicit positive test one may apply to candidate innate propositions. He subsequently argues these marks either fail or apply badly to Herbert’s own examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability test for proposed marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proposed mark of innateness must actually be found in the claimed innate propositions; failure of fit (marks not present) undermines the innateness claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume shows how Herbert’s marks do not uniformly apply to his five example propositions (e.g. 'virtue with piety is the best worship of God' poorly fits several marks). The test: check whether each mark truly characterizes the candidate principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical infancy test (ideas must appear early / in children)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an idea is innate it should be evident in newborns or children before instruction — innate ideas should be clearest in those least exposed to education and custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume insists that newborns show little evidence of settled abstract ideas beyond basic sensations; if innate principles existed they should be manifest in children or the illiterate. The absence of such manifestation counts against innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Component-ideas requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition cannot be innate unless the ideas that compose it are themselves innate; without innate component ideas there can be no innate propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that if the underlying ideas (e.g. identity, impossibility, extension, number) are not native, then the complex propositions built from them cannot be native either — so analysis of component ideas is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete-idea test (abstract mathematical/logical ideas must be accounted for)
rubrics_metrics.description: Putative innate abstract ideas (identity, impossibility, whole/part, number, extension) should be present in the mind from infancy if innate; Hume challenges this by showing these ideas are not evident in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be' and 'the whole is bigger than the part' are commonly cited as innate, but Hume questions whether ideas like identity, impossibility, whole/part are actually present without prior experience — examine whether such abstract concepts appear pre-linguistically or pre-experientially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin/psychology test (education/custom as alternative explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent 'innate' principles may instead be acquired via education, custom, and the repeated authority of caretakers and elders; test historical and psychological origins before ascribing innateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume describes how nurses, parents, and societal customs can instil doctrines early enough that people mistake them for innate ideas. Investigate whether the principle can be traced to instruction and social reinforcement rather than native imprinting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circularity / elitist-consent objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to 'universal consent' that in practice rely on the agreement of a selected class of 'men of reason' are circular and inadequate evidence for innateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume warns against the manoeuvre where advocates claim their own group's opinions represent universal consent. Scrutinize claims of universal assent for possible elitist selection or rhetorical short-cuts to infallibility.
